176.title: Az-Zalzalah: the quake
176.hook: on that Day the earth tells its news, and an atom's weight of good is seen (Surah 99)
176.howItsDone: Az-Zalzalah is recited in the prayers, and its last two verses on the atom's weight of good and ill are among the most quoted lines in Muslim teaching on small deeds.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Al-'Adiyat, the chargers, and the human who forgets his blessings. Your line was gratitude charges forward. Day one hundred seventy-six.

People who've lived through an earthquake describe the same thing first. Not the noise. The ground. The one thing you never think about, the thing that holds everything up, suddenly moving under your feet. Glasses rattle, then walls, and the floor feels like the deck of a boat. Everything you assumed was solid isn't. Today's surah opens with the whole earth shaking like that, once and for all. Then it does something tender: it zooms all the way down, to the smallest thing there is.
screen: `THE GROUND MOVES UNDER YOU.` → `NOTHING SOLID IS SOLID.` → `THEN, THE SMALLEST THING.`

segments.voice: Zalzalah is a word that shakes when you say it: zal-zala, the syllables doubling like a tremor. The surah begins: when the earth is shaken with its final quake, and throws out its burdens, and a person asks, what's wrong with it? That day it will tell its news. More on that line tomorrow. Today, the ending, which many Muslims know by heart. In Pickthall's translation: And whoso doeth good an atom's weight will see it then, And whoso doeth ill an atom's weight will see it then. The word translated atom is dharrah. In the Arabic of the time it meant a tiny ant, or a speck of dust in a sunbeam, the smallest thing a person could see. In the surah's picture, nothing gets lost. Not the big donation, and not the smile at the cashier. Not the cruel comment, and not the kind one. The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ made the same point in a hadith in Bukhari: protect yourself from the Fire, even with half a date given in charity. Half a date. And in Muslim: don't look down on any good deed, even meeting your brother with a cheerful face. This surah turns a corner. Eighteen days of the shortest surahs, read from the last page of the Qur'an backward, from An-Nas to here. From tomorrow the surahs grow a little longer. This stretch ends on the right note: an atom of good, seen.
screen: `ZALZALAH — A WORD THAT SHAKES.` · `THE EARTH THROWS OUT ITS BURDENS.` · `DHARRAH — A TINY ANT, A SPECK OF DUST.` · `EVEN HALF A DATE.` · then, large: `AN ATOM OF GOOD.`

segments.voice: Picture a dharrah: one speck of dust turning in a sunbeam. Think that small, and find one tiny good you could do in the next hour, a glass of water for someone, a kind reply, picking up one piece of litter, a smile on purpose, and picture yourself doing it. Make it so small you can't say no.
Az-Zalzalah. The quake, the final shaking of the earth, and the surah that says an atom's weight of good will be seen. Today's word.
Your line: an atom of good. The surah says even that small gets seen. Until tomorrow.

screen: `DAY 176 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: AZ-ZALZALAH AGAIN: THE EARTH'S REPORT.`

a storm that tears the sky apart

177.title: Az-Zalzalah again: the earth's report
177.hook: the ground itself will tell what was done on it (99:4–5)
177.howItsDone: Some Muslims pray their voluntary prayers in a different spot from the obligatory ones, and scholars have connected the practice with the earth bearing witness on the Day of Judgment.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Az-Zalzalah, the quake, and the atom's weight. Your line was an atom of good. Day one hundred seventy-seven.

Archaeologists can read a floor. Dig down through a site, and the dirt tells you who lived there, what they ate, where they cooked, when the fire came. A footprint pressed into mud can outlast the person who made it. The ground keeps records nobody asked it to keep. Today, back to the line in the middle of Surah az-Zalzalah, the one skipped yesterday: the earth itself as a witness. And a new stretch of the path begins, the middle surahs, a little longer, a little deeper.
screen: `ARCHAEOLOGISTS READ A FLOOR.` → `THE GROUND KEEPS RECORDS.` → `THE MIDDLE SURAHS BEGIN.`

segments.voice: On that Day, after the quake, the surah says the earth speaks. In Pickthall's translation: That day she will relate her chronicles, Because thy Lord inspireth her. Chronicles, akhbar: news, reports, the story of what happened. The earth everyone has walked on will give its account. How? The surah's answer is simple: because the Lord inspires her, tells her to. A hadith in Tirmidhi fills in the picture. The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ recited this verse and asked his companions: do you know what her news is? They said: Allah and His Messenger know best. He said: her news is that she will testify about every servant, man or woman, about what they did on her back. She'll say: he did this, on such and such a day. So every place is a witness. The kitchen where you were patient, or weren't. The sidewalk where you stepped around someone, or stopped. The office, the car, the park bench. Some scholars drew a gentle conclusion: pray in different places, so more of the earth can speak well of you. Some pray the extra prayers in a different spot from the obligatory ones, partly for this reason. Notice the tone. The ground isn't an enemy, spying. It's more like an old friend who was there the whole time, and it can remember good as easily as harm. The ground remembers.
screen: `AKHBAR — THE EARTH'S NEWS.` · `BECAUSE THY LORD INSPIRETH HER.` · `SHE TESTIFIES TO WHAT WAS DONE ON HER.` · `PRAY IN MANY PLACES.` · then, large: `THE GROUND REMEMBERS.`

segments.voice: Stand if you can, or rest your feet flat on the floor, and notice the ground holding you; ask what this spot has seen from you this week. Then take ten slow steps, as if the ground could feel each one and would remember how you walked. If you can't walk, press your feet softly into the floor, ten times.
Az-Zalzalah again. The earth's report: on that Day the ground will tell what was done on it. Today's word.
Your line: the ground remembers. Every place is a witness, and a friendly one. Day one hundred seventy-seven.

178.title: Al-Bayyinah: the clear proof
178.hook: the People of the Book and others awaited a clear sign (Surah 98)
178.howItsDone: Muslims recite al-Bayyinah in the prayers, and the hadith of the Prophet reciting it to Ubayy ibn Ka'b is often told as a sign of honor for those who learn and recite the Qur'an.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Az-Zalzalah again, the earth that tells what was done on it. Your line was the ground remembers. Day one hundred seventy-eight.

One day, the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ went to a companion named Ubayy ibn Ka'b, a man known for his recitation, and said something strange. Allah has commanded me to recite to you: those who disbelieve, the opening of Surah al-Bayyinah. Ubayy asked: did He name me? The Prophet said: yes. And Ubayy wept. It's in Sahih al-Bukhari. A man hears that his own name was spoken by the Lord of the worlds, and he cries. Of all the surahs, this was the one chosen for that moment.
screen: `RECITE IT TO UBAYY.` → `DID HE NAME ME?` → `AND UBAYY WEPT.`

segments.voice: Bayyinah means a clear proof, evidence you can see, something that makes a matter plain. The root is b-y-n, to be distinct, to stand out clearly, the same root as bayan, a clear statement. The surah opens with people waiting. Those who disbelieved among the People of the Book, a phrase commentators apply to Jews and Christians, and among the polytheists, the surah says, would not let go of their ways until the clear proof came to them. Then it names that proof: a messenger from Allah, reciting purified pages, containing upright writings. For Muslims, that's the Prophet and the Qur'an he recited. Then a quiet line: the People of the Book did not divide until after the clear proof had come to them. Commentators read it as a pattern the Qur'an describes more than once: clarity itself can become the place people disagree. A sign doesn't end argument; sometimes it starts it. In its closing verses the surah describes two kinds of people and their ends, and speaks of those who believe and do good as the best of creation, well pleased with Allah and He with them. Tomorrow, the verse in the middle, about what was actually asked of everyone. Today, just the word. A clear proof makes things plain enough to choose. The Qur'an presents itself that way: not as a riddle, but as bayyinah, something clear. What people do with clarity is another matter.
screen: `BAYYINAH — EVIDENCE YOU CAN SEE.` · `PEOPLE WAITING FOR A SIGN.` · `A MESSENGER, PURIFIED PAGES.` · `CLARITY CAN BECOME A DISPUTE.` · then, large: `CLEAR PROOF.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one short verse you've met here, like by time, or he is one, and say it once, slowly. Then think of something in your life that is actually clear, that you already know is right, and that you've been putting off anyway. Just let it be plain.
Al-Bayyinah. The clear proof, evidence that makes a matter plain; the name of Surah ninety-eight. Today's word.
Your line: clear proof. What's already clear doesn't need a bigger sign. That's day one hundred seventy-eight.

179.title: Al-Bayyinah: sincere devotion
179.hook: all they were asked was to worship Allah sincerely, pray, and give (98:5)
179.howItsDone: Muslims speak of niyyah, intention, before acts of worship, and many recall the hadith 'actions are only by intentions'; Islamic teaching encourages hiding some good deeds so they stay sincere.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Al-Bayyinah, the clear proof, and Ubayy weeping when he heard he'd been named. Your line was clear proof.

Some instructions are long. The tax form, the terms and conditions, the washing machine manual. And some are short enough to write on your hand. Yesterday's surah described people arguing and dividing, even after a clear sign had come. Then, right in the middle, it stops and says, in effect: here's all you were ever asked. One verse. A short list, with the words naught else in front of it.
screen: `SOME INSTRUCTIONS FIT ON YOUR HAND.` → `HERE'S ALL YOU WERE ASKED.` → `ONE VERSE.`

segments.voice: Verse five of Surah al-Bayyinah, in Pickthall's translation: And they are ordered naught else than to serve Allah, keeping religion pure for Him, as men by nature upright, and to establish worship and to pay the poor-due. Naught else. Nothing more than this. Look at the pieces. First, keeping religion pure for Him. The Arabic is mukhlisin, from the same root as al-Ikhlas, which we met a few weeks ago: sincerity, purity, nothing mixed in. Worship done for Allah, not for an audience or a reputation. Second, as men by nature upright: hunafa'. A hanif is someone who turns away from idols toward the one God, and the Qur'an's great example is Ibrahim. It suggests something straight, not bent by pressure. Third and fourth, prayer and giving, salah and zakah, named side by side here as in other verses: one toward Allah, one toward people. Sincere, upright, praying, giving. The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ put the first piece at the head of everything. The very first hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari says: actions are only by intentions, and each person gets only what they intended. Two people can do the same prayer, the same donation, side by side, one for Allah and the other to be seen. From the outside, identical. Inside, not the same act at all. A short list, and the first item is the one nobody else can check.
screen: `NAUGHT ELSE — THIS IS ALL.` · `MUKHLISIN — SINCERE, NOTHING MIXED IN.` · `HUNAFA' — UPRIGHT, LIKE IBRAHIM.` · `ACTIONS ARE BY INTENTIONS.` · then, large: `SINCERE AND UPRIGHT.`

segments.voice: Choose one act to do purely for Allah, or, if that's not your language, purely for the good of it: something nobody will see or thank you for, like paying for a stranger's coffee without saying so, or cleaning something that isn't yours. Then check your intention honestly, and if any part of it is for how it looks, make it quieter until it isn't.
Al-Bayyinah. The clear proof, and the surah whose center says: all that was asked is sincere, upright worship, prayer and giving. Today's word.
Your line: sincere and upright. Naught else was asked. Day one hundred seventy-nine, done.

screen: `DAY 179 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: AL-QADR: THE NIGHT OF POWER.`

180.title: Al-Qadr: the Night of Power
180.hook: angels and the Spirit descend, peace until dawn (Surah 97)
180.howItsDone: In the last ten nights of Ramadan many Muslims pray late into the night, read Qur'an and make supplication, seeking Laylat al-Qadr in the odd nights; some stay in the mosque in retreat (i'tikaf).

segments.voice: Yesterday: Al-Bayyinah, and the verse that said all that was asked: sincere, upright, praying, giving. Your line was sincere and upright.

Late in Ramadan, a mosque changes shape. In the last ten nights, the crowds grow. People who work all day come back at midnight and stay until the pre-dawn meal. Some sleep in the mosque. Children are woken up to join. They're looking for one night, and nobody knows for certain which one it is. Today's surah is five lines about that night: what it is, why it matters, and how it ends.
screen: `THE LAST TEN NIGHTS OF RAMADAN.` → `LOOKING FOR ONE NIGHT.` → `NOBODY KNOWS WHICH.`

segments.voice: Surah ninety-seven, in Pickthall's translation: Lo! We revealed it on the Night of Power. Ah, what will convey unto thee what the Night of Power is! The Night of Power is better than a thousand months. The angels and the Spirit descend therein, by the permission of their Lord, with all decrees. The night is Peace until the rising of the dawn. Tradition holds that it's the night the Qur'an was first revealed. Qadr has two meanings, and scholars keep both: power, honor, greatness; and measure, decree, the night on which matters for the year are measured out. A thousand months is about eighty-three years: one night, better than a whole life of ordinary nights. The Spirit, ar-ruh, is identified by commentators as the angel Jibril, who brought the revelation. So the sky that night is full, busy, angels descending. And yet the surah's last word on it isn't noise or power. It's salam. Peace, until the dawn. When is it? The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ said, in Bukhari: seek it in the odd nights of the last ten of Ramadan. The twenty-seventh is a night people watch especially closely, though scholars say it isn't certain, and some say it moves year to year. Some see the uncertainty as part of the gift: it keeps people awake for ten nights instead of one. Aisha asked the Prophet what she should say if she found it, and he taught her a short prayer asking Allah, who loves to pardon, to pardon her.
screen: `WE REVEALED IT ON THE NIGHT OF POWER.` · `BETTER THAN A THOUSAND MONTHS.` · `THE ANGELS AND THE SPIRIT DESCEND.` · `THE ODD NIGHTS OF THE LAST TEN.` · then, large: `PEACE UNTIL DAWN.`

segments.voice: This is a small version of waking before dawn and sitting in the dark, no phone: close your eyes or dim the lights, and picture the sky just before sunrise, very still. Let the word salam, peace, rest on each out-breath, and if you pray, ask for pardon in your own words, as Aisha was taught.
Al-Qadr. Power and decree: the night the surah says the Qur'an was revealed, better than a thousand months, peace until dawn. Today's word.
Your line: peace until dawn. Ten nights of searching, for one that ends in peace. See you tomorrow.

181.title: Al-'Alaq: the first words
181.hook: read, in the name of your Lord who created you from a clinging clot, who taught by the pen (96:1–5)
181.howItsDone: Muslims learn the story of the first revelation in the cave of Hira as part of the Prophet's life; the opening verses of Surah al-'Alaq are recited in the prayers and often quoted to honor learning.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Al-Qadr, the Night of Power, better than a thousand months. Your line was peace until dawn.

A cave, high on a mountain outside Mecca, just big enough for one person to sit. A man of about forty climbs up there often, to be alone, to think, to turn toward God, with food his wife Khadijah has packed. One night, according to Muslim tradition in the month of Ramadan, someone else is in the cave. What's spoken there becomes the first words of the Qur'an to be revealed.
screen: `A CAVE ON A MOUNTAIN.` → `SOMEONE ELSE IS IN THE CAVE.` → `THE FIRST WORDS REVEALED.`

segments.voice: The story is told by Aisha in the opening pages of Sahih al-Bukhari. The angel Jibril came to the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ in the cave of Hira and said one word: iqra'. Read, or recite. The Prophet answered: I am not a reader. The angel pressed him tight, until he could bear no more, and said again: read. Three times. Then came these words, in Pickthall's translation: Read: In the name of thy Lord who createth, Createth man from a clot. Read: And thy Lord is the Most Bounteous, Who teacheth by the pen, Teacheth man that which he knew not. 'Alaq, the word the surah is named for, means something that clings. Pickthall says clot; many translators today prefer a clinging thing, and scholars discuss the range. The point is the contrast: a human begins as something tiny and clinging, and is taught what he did not know. And notice the pen. The first revelation, to a man who said I am not a reader, is about reading and writing. In the Qur'an's very first lines, knowledge is a gift from Allah. The Prophet came down the mountain shaking, went home to Khadijah and said: cover me, cover me. She wrapped him up, listened, and told him: Allah would never disgrace you. You keep ties with family, you help the weak, you honor guests, you stand by people in hardship. The first person to believe him was the person who knew him best.
screen: `IQRA' — READ.` · `I AM NOT A READER.` · `A CLINGING THING, TAUGHT WHAT IT KNEW NOT.` · `COVER ME — AND KHADIJAH DID.` · then, large: `TAUGHT BY THE PEN.`

segments.voice: Find a pen and any paper, a receipt, the back of an envelope, or if you can't right now, trace the letters with a finger on your palm. Slowly write one thing you learned this week that you didn't know before. Then sit with it: somebody taught you that, or something did.
Al-'Alaq. The clinging thing, the name of Surah ninety-six, whose first five verses were the first of the Qur'an revealed. Today's word.
Your line: taught by the pen. Everything you know, someone or something taught you. That's day one hundred eighty-one.

screen: `DAY 181 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: AL-'ALAQ: THE ONE WHO FORBIDS.`

182.title: Al-'Alaq: the one who forbids
182.hook: the man who forbids a servant to pray, and the command to bow and draw near (96:9–19)
182.tomorrow: At-Tin: the fig and the olive
182.howItsDone: When Muslims recite or hear 96:19 many perform a prostration of recitation (sajdat al-tilawah); in the daily prayers, the prostration is often called the moment of greatest nearness to Allah.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Al-'Alaq, the first words in the cave: read. Your line was taught by the pen.

The Ka'bah in Mecca, in the early years. The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ is praying there in the open, bowing, then putting his forehead on the ground. A powerful man of Quraysh is watching, and he's furious. He tells his friends: if I see Muhammad with his face in the dust again, I'll step on his neck. The rest of Surah al-'Alaq, after the first five verses, is about this man, and about what the one praying should do.
screen: `PRAYING IN THE OPEN.` → `I'LL STEP ON HIS NECK.` → `WHAT SHOULD THE ONE PRAYING DO?`

segments.voice: The surah turns from the pen to a warning: truly, the human being oversteps when he sees himself as self-sufficient. Then: have you seen the one who forbids a servant when he prays? The surah doesn't name him. Commentators, and a hadith in Sahih Muslim, identify him as Abu Jahl, a leading opponent of the Prophet in Mecca. The hadith says he came forward to carry out his threat, then suddenly drew back, shielding himself with his hands. Asked why, he said he'd seen between himself and the Prophet a trench of fire, and terror, and wings. The surah asks him questions: what if the one praying is rightly guided? What if he commands goodness? Doesn't he know that Allah sees? Then the last verse tells the one praying what to do. In Pickthall's translation: Nay! Obey not thou him. But prostrate thyself, and draw near unto Allah. Not fight. Not argue. Not hide. Bow down, and come closer. It's counted among the verses of prostration, though the schools of law differ on it. And it lines up with a hadith in Muslim: the closest a servant is to his Lord is while in prostration. The lowest position of the body is the nearest point to Allah. The man who wanted to push a face into the dust didn't understand: that's exactly where the nearness is. That closes a week that began with the quake and an atom of good, and moved through the earth's report, the clear proof, sincerity, the Night of Power, and now the cave and its first surah, whole.
